title: Standards Are Not It
author: Zach Groshell
summary: Groshell argues that good instructional design begins with a content analysis, not a list of standards or released test items. A content analysis is the search for generative relations within a content domain and the arrangement of course content around those relations, so that teaching one underlying idea equips students to handle many untaught cases. He illustrates the concept across spelling, math facts, earth science, and U.S. history, showing how identifying the underlying "samenesses" in each domain produces courses that are more economical and generalizable. He then contrasts this with the common practice of deriving courses directly from standards documents or item banks, which are built to sample and report achievement rather than to organize a subject coherently. Skipping content analysis, he argues, produces four compounding problems: bloated instructional volume, a proliferation of competing methods, inconsistent vocabulary, and a drift toward optimizing for item-level performance rather than genuine transfer. Groshell closes by describing what content analysis should produce instead: courses organized around big ideas, tracks, and terminal skills, with standards serving only as a coverage check applied after a course is designed, not as the design source itself.
points: Introduces "content analysis" (also called a sameness analysis) as the design step that identifies generative relations within a subject so that teaching one relation lets students correctly handle items they were never directly taught.

Uses four concrete domains (spelling, math facts, earth science, and U.S. history) to show how finding underlying structure collapses large lists of discrete facts into a small set of teachable relations.

Argues that standards documents and item banks are built for sampling and reporting achievement, not for organizing a subject, so building a course directly from them skips the analysis that would make it coherent.

Identifies four downstream costs of skipping content analysis: more instructional volume, a proliferation of competing methods, inconsistent vocabulary, and design decisions that chase item-level metrics instead of generalizable strategies.
Recommends using standards only as a post-hoc coverage check, while building the course itself from an analysis organized around big ideas, tracks, and terminal skills.
quotes: A content analysis is the search for generative relations inside a content domain, and the arrangement of the content so those relations become the organizing structure of the course.
A relation is generative to the degree that learning it lets a student respond correctly to items nobody taught them.
Spelling Through Morphographs teaches 750 morphographs and 14 rules, and students can derive the spelling of over 12,000 words.

Four rules and 36 families instead of 200 items. And the families keep paying out well past the fact table, because another invisible sameness in the content is that a word problem in the primary grades is just a family with one member missing.
Convection is the big idea, and all these topics are its instances.

Slocum and Rolf (2021) name the problem directly: instructional designs derived from skill assessments tend to omit the step of identifying the generative relations that would produce the repertoire the assessments sample.
An assessment tells you which behaviors a student can perform. It does not tell you how to organize a course that is economical and intellectually rigorous.

We cannot keep setting the bar this low, where a course counts as good if someone fed a standards document to a large language model, churned out a lesson for every entry, and called the result a curriculum.
Standards are the right tool for checking coverage once a course is built. They are the wrong tool for deciding what the lessons are.
